questions.title: Find a distance from two points
questions.prompt_html:
The endpoints of a segment are \(P(-2,-2)\) and \(Q(0,0)\).

Find the exact length of \(PQ\).
questions.solution_html:
The horizontal change is \(0-(-2)=2\). The vertical change is \(0-(-2)=2\).

Pythagoras gives \(PQ^2=2^2+2^2=8\). Taking the positive square root gives \(PQ=2 \sqrt{2}\).
questions.hint_html: Square both coordinate changes and add the squares.

questions.title: Recover an endpoint from the midpoint
questions.prompt_html:
The segment \(PQ\) has endpoint \(P(-1,2)\) and midpoint \(M(\frac{1}{2},5)\).

Find the other endpoint.
questions.solution_html:
Write the missing endpoint as \((u,v)\). Then \(\frac{-1+u}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\frac{2+v}{2}=5\).

Multiply each equation by 2, then subtract the known coordinate. This gives \(u=2\) and \(v=8\), so the endpoint is \((2,8)\).
questions.hint_html: Reverse the two coordinate averages.

The segment \(PQ\) has endpoint \(P(-1,2)\) and midpoint \(M(3,-1)\).

  1. Find the other endpoint.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact length of \(PQ\).

    [2]

  3. Find the gradient of \(PQ\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Write the missing endpoint as \((u,v)\). Then \(\frac{-1+u}{2}=3\) and \(\frac{2+v}{2}=-1\).

Multiply each equation by 2, then subtract the known coordinate. This gives \(u=7\) and \(v=-4\), so the endpoint is \((7,-4)\).

(b) The horizontal change is \(7-(-1)=8\). The vertical change is \(-4-2=-6\).

Pythagoras gives \(PQ^2=8^2+\left(-6\right)^2=100\). Taking the positive square root gives \(PQ=10\).

(c) Use the same point order for both differences. The vertical change is \(-6\) and the horizontal change is \(8\).

The gradient is \(\frac{-6}{8}=- \frac{3}{4}\).
questions.hint_html: Reverse the two coordinate averages.

marking_criteria.description_html: Square both coordinate changes and add the squares.
Find the vertical change divided by the matching horizontal change.

questions.title: Recover and use an exponential model
questions.prompt_html:

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Putting \(x=0\) into the line gives \(\log_{5}y=\log_{5}6\). Undo the logarithm to obtain \(y=6\).

(b) Raise 5 to the power of each side, then use the sum in the exponent to split the product.

This gives \(y=6\times 5^{4 x}\) because \(5^{\log_{5}6}=6\).

(c) At that input, \(mx=1\), where \(m=4\) is the transformed gradient.

The model gives \(y=6\times 5^{1}=30\).

questions.title: Recover and use an exponential model
questions.prompt_html:
A model has the form \(y=Ab^x\), with \(A>0\) and \(b>0\). The graph contains \((2,27)\) and \((4,\frac{243}{4})\).

  1. Find the exact value of \(b\).

    [2]

  2. Find a formula for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact value of \(y\) at \(x=3\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) There are two steps between the x-values. Divide the later output by the earlier one to cancel \(A\).

Then \(b^2=\frac{\frac{243}{4}}{27}=\frac{9}{4}\). Taking the positive square root gives \(b=\frac{3}{2}\).

(b) Use the first reading: \(27=A(\frac{3}{2})^{2}\). Divide by \(\frac{9}{4}\) to get \(A=12\).

The model is \(y=12\times \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^x\).

(c) Use the requested exponent in the model. This gives \(y=12(\frac{3}{2})^{3}=\frac{81}{2}\).

questions.title: Recover and use an exponential model
questions.prompt_html:
Plotting \(\log_{3}y\) against \(x\) gives the line \(\log_{3}y=\frac{x}{2}+\log_{3}8\).

  1. Find the original output when the input is zero.

    [2]

  2. Find an equation for \(y\) in terms of \(x\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact value of \(y\) when \(x=2\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a) Putting \(x=0\) into the line gives \(\log_{3}y=\log_{3}8\). Undo the logarithm to obtain \(y=8\).

(b) Raise 3 to the power of each side, then use the sum in the exponent to split the product.

This gives \(y=8\times 3^{\frac{x}{2}}\) because \(3^{\log_{3}8}=8\).

(c) At that input, \(mx=1\), where \(m=\frac{1}{2}\) is the transformed gradient.

The model gives \(y=8\times 3^{1}=24\).
